docs.title: The Anatomy Theatre
docs.text:
(a working title — the anatomy theatre was the room where the anatomy lesson was taught)

This is a reading library: a small number of subjects, each built out to the depth of a good textbook. Every subject opens with an overview and a recommended reading path, then chapters you can read in order or dip into, then deep dives wherever there is real material to go further — the intent is that you can always dig a little deeper, and never hit filler.

Subjects:

  • Dance — choreographers and their works, movement vocabularies and how machines might learn them, notation, the music relationship, chance and algorithmic methods, costume and the staged body, and the fully synthetic dancer. First chapters live; more arriving in batches.
  • Minimal techno — the production craft: groove, the voices, reduction, long-form hypnosis, the artists' documented methods. Queued.

Sources and provenance sit behind tap-able footnotes at the bottom of each page — the text stays clean. Everything here is distilled from a private knowledge commons plus the general knowledge of the agents who write it; where a page draws on the commons' research notes, it says so in a collapsed Field notes block at the end.

docs.title: Dance
docs.text: Choreography solved a problem seventy years before anyone asked a machine to: how to build a limited vocabulary of movement and a set of rules that recombine it into something worth watching. This subject covers the art form whole — the traditions and their makers, the languages of movement and the systems for writing them down, the strange marriage with music, the chance procedures and algorithms, the dressed and lit body on a stage, and the fully synthetic dancer — but that solved problem is its center of gravity, and the chapters radiate out from it.

docs.title: The shape of the subject
docs.text:
Eight parts. Chapters are self-contained — you can read any one cold — but within a part they're ordered, and the parts themselves zoom from the territory down to the machinery:

  • I · The territory — what dance is and what it's for; a world atlas of everything anyone calls dance; ballet's long history; the modern revolt; street and club styles. (coming)
  • II · Movement language — how vocabularies of movement get built, taught, described, and — the open frontier — discovered by machines from video. (first chapters below)
  • III · Writing it down — Labanotation, Benesh, motif notation; video and digital scores. (coming)
  • IV · Music and dance — both directions of the marriage: choreographers using music, composers writing for bodies. (coming)
  • V · Chance, systems, algorithms — Cunningham to code: the generative tradition and the architecture it converged on. (first chapters below)
  • VI · The staged body — costume, props, environment, light. (coming)
  • VII · The synthetic dancer — the plausible body, motion capture, movement generation, rendering. (coming)
  • VIII · The shelf — reference pages on the choreographers themselves. (coming)

docs.title: Available now
docs.text:
From Movement language:

  • Building a gamut — how a piece-specific movement vocabulary is actually assembled: units, state, operators, and the traps between them.
  • Effort and quality — Laban's answer to a question most vocabularies forget to ask: not what the body does, but how.

From Chance, systems, algorithms:

  • Chance and rule-based choreography — Cunningham's coin tosses, Brown's accumulations, Childs's permutations, Halprin's cycles: what seventy years of generative choreography actually did, and the two-layer architecture all of it shares.
  • The gamut+rules architecture — the engineering synthesis: transition legality, the three transition policies, the human gate, and why the rendering of a machine's proposal is a design decision.

A sensible first read is those four in that order — the two language chapters set up terms the two systems chapters use heavily.

docs.title: Building a gamut
docs.text:
Choreographers rarely make dances out of "movement" in general. They make a gamut — a finite, named set of movement units built for one piece — and then compose with that. The word is Cunningham's, borrowed from music, and the practice is close to universal even among choreographers who'd never use the term: Trisha Brown's Primary Accumulation is thirty movements; Cunningham's Torse is sixty-four phrases expanded from five torso positions; Lucinda Childs built entire works from a single step pattern permuted through space. If you've ever designed a synth patch bank for one track, or a constrained palette for one visual piece, you know the move: the vocabulary is a composition decision, made before composing begins.

This chapter is about how that vocabulary gets built well — which turns out to be a genuine design discipline with named failure modes, most of them invisible until you try to recombine the units and things break. The dance tradition worked these problems out by hand over decades; the same lessons apply directly if the thing recombining your units is a rule system or a model.

docs.title: Start from a coverage checklist, not from taste
docs.text:
The naive way to build a vocabulary is to improvise material until you have "enough," then name what you kept. The predictable result is a set that clusters around its author's habits — twenty units that are secretly five, all sharing a dynamic range, a level, a relationship to weight. Any generator downstream (human or machine) can then only recombine within that cluster.

The corrective is an independent checklist of movement classes, scored against your set. The best-established one is Ann Hutchinson Guest's Movement Alphabet1: a claimed-complete list of fifteen "prime actions from which all movement derives," in six groups — any action, stillness · flexion, extension, rotation · travelling, direction · support, spring · balance, falling · motion toward, motion away, destination, any form of relating. Treat completeness as a strong pedagogical claim rather than a theorem (it has been taught for forty years, which counts for something), and it becomes exactly what a vocabulary-builder needs: fill the empty cells, and your set spans the space of movement instead of sampling one corner.

Look closely at the list, though, and five of the fifteen aren't performable actions at all. Motion toward, motion away, destination, and form of relating are specification modes — ways of defining a movement (by its trajectory, by its endpoint, by its relationship) rather than movements themselves. Strip those out and the performable core is about ten verb classes: travel, turn, spring, gesture into a direction, flex, extend, transfer weight, balance, fall, be still. Ten verbs sounds small. It's the right order of magnitude — the historical gamuts that worked are all counted in dozens, never hundreds, a point the systems chapters return to with the receipts.

docs.title: State-changing verbs must be first-class units
docs.text:
The subtlest thing about Guest's alphabet is what it chooses to promote. Support (a weight transfer), balance, and falling are alphabet entries — full verbs — rather than adverbs or transitions hiding between other moves. That looks like a taxonomic quirk and is actually the deepest design rule in the chapter:

anything that changes state that other units will read deserves its own named unit.

Fall is the canonical case. A fall isn't just a shape in time — it writes state: the body ends off-balance, with momentum, and only certain movements can legally happen next. If your vocabulary treats falling as something that just happens inside transitions, no rule system can see that state, and sequences will be generated that a body cannot perform. Worse, falls create an obligation: for every direction your vocabulary can fall, it needs at least one recovery unit that reads the off-balance state and resolves it. A vocabulary with falls and no recoveries deadlocks — the generator paints the dancer into corners.

This is a special case of a distinction worth making for the whole set: which units are atomic (self-contained, no dependencies — a gesture, a turn in place) and which are entangled (they read or write state that other units depend on — falls, catches, weight transfers, anything with momentum). Atomic units can be recombined freely. Entangled units need their dependencies declared, or recombination breaks in ways that only show up two units downstream. Map this before composing, not after.

And one more promotion from the alphabet worth honoring: stillness is an item, not a gap. A rest is a unit with duration, level, and shape — Cage's lesson transplanted to the body. It also happens to be the single most useful edit point when movement is destined for camera, which is worth remembering the moment your dancers are synthetic.

docs.title: Give every unit a type signature
docs.text:
The practical form of "declare the dependencies" is borrowed from programming: give each unit a type signature — what it requires to begin (preconditions) and what's true when it ends (postconditions). For movement, six fields cover the state that matters:

Field What it records support which base bears weight — feet, one foot, seat, back, hands+feet… level floor / low / mid / standing / air balance balanced, suspended, off-balance (and which way) momentum magnitude and direction, including rotational facing relative orientation change, never absolute free limbs what's available for the next unit to use

Then unit B may follow unit A exactly when A's postconditions satisfy B's preconditions, field by field, with wildcards where a unit genuinely doesn't care. Legality stops being a judgment call and becomes checkable by inspection — which is the entire foundation the gamut+rules architecture builds on.

Two field-specific notes, both earned the hard way. Weight is the treacherous field: dance pedagogy independently names incomplete weight transfer as the root cause of most transition failures, so annotate support changes with special care. And facing must be stored relative — a unit that "ends facing stage left" is really a unit that ends rotated 90° from where it began; store the absolute version and you'll reject joins that were fine and duplicate units to compensate.

One honest caveat from the notation world: every system surveyed, Guest's included, carries a standing bias. If floorwork matters to your vocabulary — and in contemporary movement it will — don't inherit a default support list; name the floor supports explicitly (back, side, seat, hands-and-feet) as first-class values.

docs.title: The operator layer: transforms, not more units
docs.text:
A gamut of a few dozen units would exhaust itself quickly if units were all there was. The second layer is operators: transformations applied to units to generate variants. Dance pedagogy converged on a remarkably stable catalog decades ago — Blom & Chaplin's sixteen ways to manipulate a motif2 (repetition, retrograde, inversion, size, tempo, rhythm, quality, instrumentation, force, background, staging, embellishment, change of level, additive, fragmentation, combination), with William Forsythe's ~thirty geometric operations — extension, extrusion, folding, bridging, avoidance, reorientation, compression — as the improvisation-side twin.3

The structural fact that matters more than either list: operators are material-independent. Forsythe's catalog reads like a graphics API precisely because it applies to whatever the dancer already knows — the vocabulary and the operator set are orthogonal layers. That's why roughly thirty concepts constitute a literacy a practitioner internalizes rather than a repertoire they memorize, and it's the standard to hold your own operators to: an operator that only works on one unit isn't an operator, it's a variant that snuck into the wrong layer.

Two constraints keep an operator layer sound:

  • Closure — applying any operator to legal material must yield legal material. An operator that can produce output outside the vocabulary's own rules poisons everything downstream.
  • Survivability — the operand must remain itself under the transform. A reaching curve compresses beautifully; a walking step compresses into nonsense. Part of authoring a unit is knowing which operators it survives.

docs.title: Not all operators are equally automatable
docs.text:
If a rule system (or an agent) will be applying these operators, the catalog needs one more sorting: by mechanizability — how much judgment the operator secretly requires. The sixteen sort cleanly into three tiers:

  • Tier 1 — fully mechanical. Repetition ×n, tempo change including freeze, re-facing and relocation, level transposition, mirroring, size augmentation/diminution, retrograde. Safe to auto-apply.
  • Tier 2 — mechanical plus a light curation pass. Fragmentation (take the first, middle, or last third), re-accenting within the same duration, flipping one effort quality bit, instrumentation (move the phrase to a different body part — undefined for weight-bearing units), appending an ornament.
  • Tier 3 — judgment-heavy. Whole-quality reimagining, inversion, redesigning the background behind a motif, stacking several operators at once. Offer these as prompts to a human; don't auto-apply them.

The tiering isn't invented — it's empirical. Every teaching syllabus carries tiers 1–2; only the full scholarly catalog carries tier 3. And it comes with a trap worth framing on the wall: mechanizable to specify is not the same as feasible to execute. Retrograde is the cleanest tier-1 operator on paper and one of the hardest things a body can be asked to do with any unit that bears weight or carries momentum — playing a fall backwards is not a fall. A catalog inherited from pedagogy encodes what a trained human can be asked to attempt, not what a generator can safely emit; check every "mechanical" operator against the physics before trusting its tier, and restrict the rough ones to gesture-dominant material.

docs.title: What a finished gamut looks like
docs.text:
Pulling the threads together, a well-built gamut is:

  1. Small — dozens of units, chosen, not harvested;
  2. Spanning — scored against an independent class list, empty cells filled deliberately;
  3. Stateful — state-changing verbs promoted to first-class units, entanglements mapped, every fall paired with recoveries;
  4. Typed — each unit carrying pre/postconditions over support, level, balance, momentum, relative facing, free limbs;
  5. Transformable — a separate, closed operator layer, tiered by how much judgment each operator hides.

None of this yet says how units get sequenced, what makes a chain of them legal in practice, or who judges the result — that's the architecture chapter. And the question of how a unit is performed, as opposed to what it is, has its own axis entirely: effort and quality, next.

Field notes

This chapter renders the following commons notes: theory-movement-alphabet-primitives (the Movement Alphabet as coverage checklist; state changes as first-class), structure-typed-composable-primitives (type signatures; pre/post legality), structure-atomic-vs-entangled-primitives (entanglement mapping; the fall/recovery deadlock), structure-operator-mechanizability-tiers (the operator catalog, tiering, and the retrograde trap).

  1. Ann Hutchinson Guest, The Movement Alphabet (Language of Dance Centre). Guest — the century's foremost dance-notation scholar — distilled it from a lifetime of Labanotation work; it underpins her Motif Notation, which returns in the notation chapters. ↩

  2. Anne Green Gilbert–era pedagogy standardized many operator lists, but the canonical sixteen are from Lynne Anne Blom & L. Tarin Chaplin, The Intimate Act of Choreography (1982) — still the standard composition textbook. ↩

  3. William Forsythe, Improvisation Technologies: A Tool for the Analytical Dance Eye (ZKM, 1999) — the CD-ROM in which Forsythe draws his operations as white lines over video of his own body; it reappears in the digital-scores chapter. ↩

docs.title: Effort and quality
docs.text:
Watch two dancers perform the same phrase — same steps, same counts, same shapes — and you can still see, instantly, that they are doing different things. One presses through the movement as if the air were honey; the other flicks through it like shooing insects. Everything in the previous chapter — units, signatures, operators — describes what the body does. This chapter is about the axis that describes how, which turns out to be separable from the what, nameable, and — the reason it earns a chapter — astonishingly well-engineered.

The engineering is Rudolf Laban's. A Hungarian-born movement theorist working in Weimar Germany and later wartime England, Laban built the twentieth century's most systematic analysis of human movement — Labanotation, the symbolic score system, is his (it gets its own chapter), and so is the analytical framework now taught as Laban Movement Analysis. The piece of it that matters here is the category he called Effort: a factored decomposition of movement quality, the dynamic, expressive dimension that survives when you subtract the choreography.1

docs.title: Four factors, two poles each
docs.text:
Laban's claim is that quality decomposes into four independent bipolar factors, each of which he tied to an inner attitude:

Factor Poles Inner attitude Space direct ↔ indirect attention Weight strong ↔ light intention Time sudden ↔ sustained decision Flow bound ↔ free progression

Direct movement channels toward a single point (a dart's flight); indirect attends everywhere at once (a fly's). Strong engages weight forcefully; light nearly denies it. Sudden is urgent, sustained is unhurried. Bound flow can be stopped at any instant; free flow is committed — launched, ballistic, unstoppable without a recovery.

Any factored system invites the same question you'd ask of a synth: what do the combinations sound like? Take the first three factors as binary and you get eight combinations, and this is where Laban's system shows its craftsmanship — all eight have names, and the names are vivid enough to teach:

sudden, direct sudden, indirect sustained, direct sustained, indirect strong punch slash press wring light dab flick glide float

These are the eight effort actions, and the table above is the canonical assignment — worth stating plainly because actor-training materials garble it constantly.2 Each name is a compressed lesson: you already know, in your arm, the difference between wring (strong, sustained, indirect — a towel) and press (strong, sustained, direct — a stamp), and that kinesthetic memory is doing the work a paragraph of description would fail at.

docs.title: The cube, and distance for free
docs.text:
Now the property that makes Effort more than a nice taxonomy. Three binary factors put the eight actions on the corners of a cube — and cube adjacency is a metric. Two actions differing in one factor are neighbors: punch → press changes only Time, and reads as development, a modulation of the same idea. Flip all three factors — punch → float — and you have maximal contrast, the movement equivalent of a subito pianissimo.

If you build generative systems, that sentence should have lit up: this is a modifier axis that ships with its own distance function. "Vary it a little" versus "contrast hard" stops being a taste call and becomes a Hamming distance — 1 bit is development, 3 bits is rupture. The pedagogy even hands you an anti-monotony rule ready for mechanization: never let more than two consecutive phrases share an effort signature. That's a constraint a rule system can enforce while remaining wholly agnostic about which movements it's shaping — a dynamic arc drawn with no new machinery at all.

And it layers cleanly. The proof is a computer-animation classic: the EMOTE model implemented Effort as four continuous dials in [−1, +1] that modulate the timing curves and trajectory shape of independently authored base gestures.3 Quality as a pure multiplier over material defined elsewhere — the modifier ideal from the operator layer, demonstrated at animation-production quality in the year 2000. When a vocabulary keeps what and how in separate layers, one gamut of a few dozen units times eight qualities times a couple of intensity levels yields a combinatorial space in the thousands, every point of it nameable.

docs.title: Flow is not like the others
docs.text:
You'll have noticed the eight actions use only three factors. Flow, the fourth, is deliberately excluded — and the reason generalizes into a design rule.

Bound flow means the movement can be arrested at any moment; free flow means it can't — the dancer has committed momentum that must land somewhere. That isn't a color of the movement. It's a postcondition: a fact about what can legally happen next. A free-flow leap doesn't merely feel different from a bound-flow reach — it constrains the successor unit in a way no quality should. Which is why Flow belongs in the type signature — in the momentum and balance fields of the unit's pre/post contract, feeding the transition checks of the architecture chapter — while Weight, Time, and Space stay in the palette as pure style.

The rule underneath: when a "quality" changes what may follow, it isn't a quality — it's state. Sort your axes by that test and both layers stay honest.

docs.title: What effort is not
docs.text:
Two boundaries keep the system from being oversold.

Effort values are performance targets, not measurables. Inter-rater reliability between trained Laban observers is only moderate; no checker, human or algorithmic, can verify that a movement was performed with "wringing" quality. This isn't a flaw to engineer away — it defines where the axis lives. In the division of labor the gamut+rules chapter makes precise, mechanical state — support, level, momentum — is the machine's tier, and quality is irreducibly the human's tier: a target you set, a judgment you render, never a value you assert was achieved.

The vocabulary is a convention, not the only one. Modern-dance pedagogy commonly teaches six movement qualities instead — sustained, percussive, swinging, suspended, collapsing, vibratory — and Ohad Naharin's Gaga (his movement language for Batsheva) works in texture words: float, quake, melt, groove. Both map, roughly, onto the same underlying axis Laban factored. The practical advice: pick the naming your performers already speak; keep the cube underneath for the machinery.

docs.title: The transferable lesson
docs.text:
Strip away the dance and Effort is a masterclass in designing any modifier axis: prefer a product of a few binary factors over a flat list of adjectives. A flat adjective list — "make it aggressive, dreamy, punchy, mellow…" — grows without structure, overlaps without warning, and gives you no notion of near or far. A factored product gives you orthogonality by construction, a built-in distance metric, and — if you name the corners well — memorable handles that teach themselves. Eight named cells from three bits is a better interface than thirty unstructured adjectives, whether the thing being modified is a phrase of movement, a synth patch, or a generated shot.

Laban got there in the 1940s, for bodies. It has yet to be improved on.

Field notes

This chapter renders the commons note theory-laban-effort-quality-axis (the effort cube as a modifier axis with a free contrast metric; Flow as type-signature state; EMOTE as layerability proof; quality as performance target, not measurable).

  1. Laban's own presentation is The Mastery of Movement (1950, revised with Lisa Ullmann); Effort was first systematized with F. C. Lawrence in Effort (1947), a wartime study of industrial movement efficiency — the factory floor, oddly, is where the expressive vocabulary was forged. ↩

  2. "Punch" appears in some sources as "thrust" — same cell, same action. ↩

  3. Diane Chi, Monica Costa, Liwei Zhao & Norman Badler, "The EMOTE Model for Effort and Shape," SIGGRAPH 2000. Badler's Center for Human Modeling and Simulation at Penn spent decades making Laban computable. ↩

docs.title: Chance and rule-based choreography
docs.text:
In the early 1950s, Merce Cunningham began deciding parts of his dances by tossing coins. It remains one of the most misunderstood acts in twentieth-century art — misread then as abdication, misread now as a quaint precursor to "generative art." What Cunningham actually built, and what Trisha Brown, Lucinda Childs, Anna Halprin, and the Fluxus artists built after him, was a body of working generative systems with documented mechanisms, documented sizes, and documented failure modes — a seventy-year experimental record on exactly the question every generative practitioner faces: which decisions do you keep, and which do you hand to the system?

The record has a shape. Learn the shape and you can skip a decade of rediscovering it.

docs.title: Cunningham: chance decides continuity, never material
docs.text:
Cunningham's procedure, developed with John Cage and stabilized by Suite by Chance (1953), ran on charts. Before any randomness entered, he composed charts of movement material by hand — one chart of phrases, and separate charts for the questions he was willing to let chance answer: sequence, duration, direction, which dancer, how many. Then coin tosses (later hexagrams from the I Ching, later dice and card draws) indexed into the charts.1

The division of labor is the whole point, and Cunningham stated both halves in the same breath. The famous axiom — "it is possible for anything to follow anything else" — is remembered; the constraint that made it work is not: the charts, he was explicit, were not made by chance. The movement in each cell was chosen. Chance was permitted to decide continuity — order, duration, spacing, assignment — and was never once, in the entire half-century record, permitted to invent material.

The mature works show the system at scale. Torse (1976) draws its title from its method: sixty-four phrases — the I Ching's number, which became his default gamut size — expanded from five torso positions, with hexagram draws determining sequence and spatial distribution. Canfield (1969) dealt its structure from the card game of the same name, fifty-two motions for fifty-two cards. The numbers matter, and here is the first structural regularity of the whole tradition: every gamut in the record is counted in dozens. Three phrases and one operator in Brown's Solo Olos. Twenty-seven points in Locus. Thirty movements in Primary Accumulation. Sixty-four in Torse. Hundreds is not a bigger version of this — it is a different and worse thing. When Forsythe once built a 135-item alphabet for a single solo, keeping it usable required the kinesphere itself as a memory palace.

docs.title: The systems generation: Brown, Childs, Halprin, Fluxus
docs.text:
The choreographers who came out of Judson Dance Theater in the 1960s kept Cunningham's architecture and swapped the stochastic layer for deterministic rules — and in doing so demonstrated that the architecture never depended on randomness at all.

Trisha Brown made the rule itself the dance. Accumulation (1971): perform gesture 1; then 1, 2; then 1, 2, 3 — an additive list executed with the patience of a proof. Locus (1975) encoded a paragraph of autobiography as numbers (A=1 … Z=26) mapped onto twenty-seven points of an imaginary cube around her body; the text drove which point she gestured toward. Same two layers as Cunningham — a small authored gamut, a mechanical sequencer — but the sequencer is a readable algorithm rather than a coin.2

Lucinda Childs fixed nearly everything and permuted the little that remained. Calico Mingling (1973): forty six-count phrases over a vocabulary of essentially one step, walked through path permutations across four dancers — canon, phase, interference, the Steve Reich move performed by bodies (and a decade before she and Reich shared a stage with Einstein on the Beach's creative orbit).

Anna Halprin, on the West Coast and a generation earlier than Judson (she taught several of its founders on her outdoor deck), contributed the meta-system. The RSVP Cycles, formalized with her husband, landscape architect Lawrence Halprin: Resources (the material available), Scores (instructions of deliberately chosen openness), Valuaction (a scheduled stage for judging what the score produced), Performance — then cycle.3 Two ideas here outlived the acronym: that a score's openness is a dial — Halprin placed every score explicitly on an open↔closed continuum — and that evaluation is a named, scheduled stage of the system rather than something that happens ambiently. The next chapter builds its human gate directly on that second idea.

Fluxus supplied the limit case of openness. George Brecht's event scores — cards from the Water Yam box, often one line ("Drip Music: a source of dripping water and an empty vessel are arranged so that the water falls into the vessel") — are scores pared to almost pure frame, to be realized "publicly, privately, or negatively." Movement-prompt decks in use today (fifty-six to seventy cards is the standard range) are this idea, commercialized.

docs.title: The architecture all of it shares
docs.text:
Line the systems up and one architecture appears in every single one:

A gamut — a finite, named, human-authored set of units — plus a sequencer that decides only continuity: order, duration, tempo, placement, facing, assignment, density, entrances and exits.

Three design decisions, made separately, define every system in the record:

1. The unit list, by hand. Crisp boundaries, each unit masterable in isolation, none requiring a particular predecessor. (How to build that list well is the gamut chapter.)

2. Exactly which dimensions the sequencer owns — enumerated in advance. This is the deepest lesson, and the least obvious. Cunningham pre-wrote, per work, the list of questions chance would be asked; the list varied, and the variance was the composition. And every strong system randomizes few dimensions and fixes the rest: Cunningham fixed the units, freed continuity; Brown fixed the sequence rule, freed body-part choice; Childs fixed everything but the path permutation; Halprin fixed the frame, freed everything inside it. Each dimension handed over multiplies unfamiliarity — when Cunningham stacked independent draws per body part, the resulting material was, in his own account, nearly impossible, and cost months of rehearsal to weld. Free every dimension and you haven't built a more generative system — you've built improvisation. That isn't a sneer: the Grand Union (the improvisational collective that emerged when Judson veterans loosened every constraint at once) is the documented instance of the transition, and the point at which the practice stops being composition in any repeatable sense.

3. When the draw happens. At authoring time, frozen thereafter — Cunningham's default: chance composed the piece, then the piece was rehearsed and toured as fixed repertory. Or live at showtime — his Field Dances gave dancers in-performance choices, and that is a different genre with different failure modes, not a braver version of the same one.

The claim underneath all three, and the tradition's central finding: a generator's leverage comes from the separation, not from the randomness. Chance, rule, algorithm, model — the sequencer technology changed four times across the record, and it never much mattered. What mattered was that material stayed authored, small, and bounded while continuity stayed free.

docs.title: Can the audience read the rule?
docs.text:
Set two of these systems side by side and a second design axis appears. Watch Accumulation for sixty seconds and you get it — the additive rule becomes legible, and from then on you're watching two things at once: the movement, and a composition materializing in real time (plus a third: the performer's visible labor of memory). Watch a Cunningham chance sequence and no amount of attention reveals a rule, because the generating structure is statistical — what observers report instead is strangeness: sequences that feel, in a way audiences struggled to articulate, inevitable rather than arbitrary, freed as they are from a choreographer's habits of what should follow what. And Yvonne Rainer's Trio A (1966) is the tradition's control experiment: a dance built to refuse every compositional recursion at once — no repetition, no accumulation, no climax, deliberately uniform dynamics — and with it, the audience's perceived structure drops to zero, on purpose.4

So: rule legibility is a per-section design decision, independent of quality. A legible rule buys a second layer of audience attention — disproportionately valuable when the surface is thin (one dancer, one voice, one instrument, one screen). An opaque rule buys inevitability and strangeness, and asks the surface to carry all the interest itself. Make the choice by default and generative work reads as arbitrary; that's usually the actual diagnosis behind the complaint.

The legible mechanisms, usefully, are the cheap ones — additive and subtractive lists, retrograde, rotation, phase, exhaustive permutation of a tiny lexicon. And the tradition's answer to their predictability is not added noise, which destroys readability immediately, but layering a second legible system: Accumulation with Talking runs two accumulations and two spoken stories simultaneously; the group Accumulation phase-shifts one material across four bodies. Two readable rules interfere; interference is interesting; readability survives.

docs.title: Scores that are deliberately incomplete
docs.text:
There's a third lever, subtler than the other two, that this tradition pulls constantly: emit an unfinished instruction, and let the performer finish it.

Brecht's one-line cards are the pure case, but the move is everywhere. Laban's own Motif Notation — the stripped-down cousin of Labanotation, using Guest's Movement Alphabet — exists precisely to record only the leading intention ("travel, then turn, ending enclosed") and leave every other dimension free: a score that is literally a program with free variables. The contemporary systems make the purpose explicit. Scuddle (2011) evolves "movement catalysts" — a body position, a height level, effort qualities, and deliberately no path between them — scored by Laban-derived heuristics, with the stated goal of breaking the choreographer's habits. Kate Sicchio's Terpsicode projects keyframes and leaves the dancer to tween them.

Why this is the cheapest robust pattern in the whole toolkit: the three hardest problems in recombining movement — legal transitions, stylistic coherence, physical feasibility — are delegated in a single move to the one person who was going to execute the result anyway. Nothing else solves three problems with one decision.

But the record is equally clear about when it pays, and the conditions bite:

  • The axes you do specify must collide with habit. Under-specify along dimensions the performer is fluent in and they hand you their defaults back — novelty pressure has to land where the habits live, which is Scuddle's entire design.
  • Openness is a dial, set per section — Halprin's continuum, or Nancy Stark Smith's Underscore (the contact-improvisation frame), which sets the dial differently in each of its twenty-plus named phases.
  • It trades machine control for human competence. The pattern needs a performer whose completion beats your rule. With no performer in the loop — a fully synthetic pipeline — this lever mostly isn't available, and everything it delegated comes back on the system's plate.

docs.title: Old news, in the best way
docs.text:
One closing reframe. This chapter's architecture — a fixed, checkable frame; a free, skilled realization inside it — is not a 1950s invention. It is how much of the world's music has always specified itself: a jazz standard's changes against the solo, a raga's grammar against the alap, flamenco's compás against the cante, a dub riddim against its versions. Traditions discovered again and again that you don't specify the piece — you specify a space of performances, as a constraint system plus a convention for filling it. Cunningham's charts and Halprin's scores are dance finding the same split, and stating it unusually plainly.

Which is encouraging, if you're building such a system: you are not imitating a mid-century avant-garde experiment. You are implementing one of the oldest architectures in performance — with, for the first time, a sequencer that can check its own work. How it checks is the next chapter.

Field notes

This chapter renders the commons notes structure-gamut-plus-sequencer (the two-layer finding, gamut sizes, dimension discipline, draw timing), structure-legible-rule-as-content (legibility as a per-section axis; Trio A as control; layering legible systems), interaction-deliberate-under-specification (Scuddle/Terpsicode/Motif; the three delegated problems; the paying conditions), theory-open-form-improvisation-frameworks (frame vs realization across musical traditions), and theory-variation-development-strategies (variation as distinct mechanisms — the operator-catalog connection).

  1. The primary scholarship this account leans on is Carrie Noland's Coping and Choreography, which reconstructs the chart procedures from Cunningham's notes and Remy Charlip's and Carolyn Brown's first-hand accounts. ↩

  2. Brown's own gloss on this period of her work: "choreography as a system that makes dance happen" — she considered the three system families (accumulations, mathematical procedures, and equipment pieces) distinct instruments. ↩

  3. Lawrence & Anna Halprin, The RSVP Cycles: Creative Processes in the Human Environment (1969) — written as a general theory of scoring for any collaborative process; dance was its proving ground. ↩

  4. Rainer's accompanying "No Manifesto" (1965) — "No to spectacle no to virtuosity…" — is the position paper; Trio A is its executable. ↩

docs.title: The gamut+rules architecture
docs.text: The previous chapter read seventy years of generative choreography as a record; this one reads it as a specification. Suppose you accept its findings — material authored and small, continuity handed to a sequencer, dimensions enumerated — and set out to build such a system today, with a typed gamut in hand. Three problems remain, and they are where the real engineering lives: what makes a chain of units legal, who judges whether a legal chain is any good, and — least obvious — what form the system's proposals should take. Each has a documented answer.

docs.title: Transitions are the hard part — and they are content
docs.text:
Start with the pedagogy's blunt correction to how engineers instinctively frame this. Transitions are not glue between the real material. Dance teaching is explicit that a transition is material — it can be a breath, a weight shift, or an entire traveling passage whose job is repositioning — and Cunningham went further: "dynamics in movement come from the continuity." The joins are where the expressive interest concentrates, not where it's absent.

Two practical facts ride along with this reframe. First, the expensive transitions are the ones that change level or support — floor to standing, standing to air. They dominate rehearsal time in the human case and failure rates in the synthetic one, so keep level-changing units a minority of the gamut and rate-limit them per phrase. Second, transitions start early: in an eight-count phrase the transition typically begins around count six or seven — the last beats of a unit are already preparation for the next. A system that treats units as sealed blocks meeting at instantaneous boundaries has mismodeled the material from the start.

Structurally, the consequence is that a vocabulary should partition into content units and connector units — weight shifts, pivots, breath suspensions, rises and lowers, rolls — whose declared job is satisfying somebody else's preconditions. Hold that thought; it becomes the fix of choice below.

docs.title: Three transition policies
docs.text:
Any system that recombines authored units makes a policy decision about joins — usually by accident. The record contains exactly three policies, and the crucial fact about them: they are per-section choices, not system-level ones.

1. The legality graph. Annotate every unit's entry and exit state; generate only legal walks. Smooth, scalable, the animation industry's default, and the only policy that works with no human in the loop. Cost: the annotation work, plus one system-level check covered below.

2. The neutral hub. Define a common neutral — a stand, a home position — and route every join through it. Always legal, zero annotation. This is what movement-prompt decks and accumulation practice do implicitly. Cost: every join has the same shape, the result is rhythmically flat, and the hub becomes a visible tic. (You have heard this failure: it is the generative-music equivalent of returning to the tonic between every phrase.)

3. Illegal by design. Cunningham's position, held deliberately: anything may follow anything, and solving the impossible joins in rehearsal is the expressive content. The costs are documented with unusual precision — Changeling took months; dancers mastered units in isolation and then welded them; Carolyn Brown described the only viable coping strategy as "absolute concentration on each single moment." So is the payoff: audiences reported chance sequences over a good gamut as reading inevitable, where conventionally structured work "looks contrived." Choose this policy knowingly, and cap unit difficulty so the welds stay humanly solvable. With synthetic dancers, note, the rehearsal room where impossible joins get solved does not exist.

docs.title: Mechanics of the legality graph
docs.text:
For policy 1, the definitive recipe comes from an unexpected direction: Motion Graphs, the SIGGRAPH 2002 paper that taught game animation how to stitch mocap clips.1 Its four mechanics transfer to any system that concatenates authored units — the paper is about pixels, but the findings are about joins.

Compare a window, not an instant. Naive per-frame pose distance fails, because a good join must match velocities and accelerations, not just positions. The paper's fix: compare the material over a window of roughly a third of a second, which makes the derivatives implicit in the comparison. General form: define the join metric over a window of the signal and derivative continuity comes free.

Quotient out what the domain leaves free. A motion clip is the same motion anywhere on the floor and facing any direction, so the distance is minimized over that free transform before comparing. Consequence for your gamut's type signatures: facing is stored relative, never absolute — only rotational momentum genuinely constrains a successor. Every domain has such a symmetry (in music it is transposition), and failing to quotient it out means rejecting valid joins and duplicating your library to compensate.

Set thresholds by audience expertise, not globally. The paper's own example: walking demands exacting joins because every viewer is an expert on walking; ballet is more forgiving because they aren't. Read that twice — it means join tolerance is a perceptual parameter, per category of material. Pedestrian connectors (walk, stand, turn) need the cleanest joins in your entire set; stylized material grants slack.

Prune to the largest strongly connected component. Pairwise legality is not enough: a graph can be locally correct and still contain sinks — states with legal entries and no legal exits — where generation stalls. Keep only the largest strongly connected component, and when it comes out too small, add connector units rather than loosening the metric. A gamut of brilliant content units with no connectors fails this check no matter how good the units are; the fix is never to redefine legality, it is to hire more of the units whose job is joining.

One adjustment when the executor is human rather than a renderer: a dancer out-blends any interpolator, so tune the thresholds permissive and let the performer legalize marginal joins. The structure transfers; the numbers don't.

docs.title: The human gate
docs.text:
Here is the finding the generative-art literature keeps treating as an embarrassment, restated as the load-bearing component it is: every system in the seventy-year record that produced kept work has a human accept/reject gate. Cunningham "almost always" refined what chance handed him. Halprin's RSVP Cycles schedules the gate as a named stage — valuaction — which is precisely what makes it a cycle rather than a one-shot generator. Wayne McGregor's Living Archive (the machine-learning collaboration with Google) proposes thirty continuations per pose; the dancers select. Curation is designed in. It is not a confession that the generator is weak.

Cunningham's gate is worth studying in detail, because he stated his criteria, and they are two different kinds of check: aesthetic interest — does the sequence read as a necessary, integral form — and practicality — can human beings perform it, in this space. A candidate can be interesting-but-impossible or performable-but-dull, and knowing which gate rejected it tells you which knob to turn upstream. Keep the criteria separate in your own gate, even if one person applies both.

The architecture that falls out is a clean two-tier split:

  • The machine tier checks whatever is stateful and enumerable. For movement: the support/level/balance/momentum/facing chain — the legality graph above. Cheap, exhaustive, and blessedly tasteless.
  • The human tier judges quality and interest — plus everything the domain defines as a performance target rather than a measurable. Effort qualities are the clean example: no checker can verify a "wringing" quality, and pretending otherwise just launders taste through a metric.

Blurring the tiers fails in exactly two directions, both worth naming. Train a learned "is-it-good" scorer and start optimizing against it, and you get the classic Goodhart collapse — the score improves while the work degrades. Or keep tightening the mechanical checker to encode taste it cannot see, and it starts rejecting joins a performer would have absorbed without noticing. The machine tier's job is to be strong and dumb: strict about state, silent about quality.

And a budgeting rule that sounds trivial and decides projects: a gate is only load-bearing if somebody sits at it. Cunningham filtered every draw; RSVP schedules valuaction; a proposal stream nobody selects from is a firehose, not a system. Size the generator's output to the number of candidates a human can actually judge, and let the machine tier guarantee nothing obviously invalid ever reaches them.

docs.title: The proposal is an interface
docs.text:
The last finding is the one nobody expects, and it may be the most transferable: the representation a system proposes in carries the same design weight as the model doing the proposing.

Exhibit one. The Choreographic Language Agent — built by Marc Downie's OpenEndedGroup for Wayne McGregor's company — renders its choreographic proposals as animated constructions of points, lines, and planes, deliberately not as an anatomical avatar. The stated reason: dancers imitate a realistic figure literally, but are forced to interpret an abstract sketch. Fidelity of rendering directly sets how much the human contributes. Want the human's job to be selection? Render high-fidelity, so they judge the real thing. Want their job to be completion — the under-specification lever — render deliberately lossy, and lossy in the dimensions you want them to own.

Exhibit two, the cautionary one. Cunningham spent his last two decades composing with LifeForms, early choreography software whose avatar was divided into fourteen independently keyframeable sections. Critics can date works of that era on sight: angular arm material running in counter-rhythm against the legs — because independent per-limb layering was the cheap operation, and the tool's easiest path quietly became the house style. Nobody chose that. Whatever your tool makes one-click will show up in the artifacts; audit the easy path as a style decision, not a convenience.

Corollary, for high-fidelity previews: they defer the feasibility check, they don't perform it. LifeForms happily rendered sequences that were physically impossible, and the impossibility surfaced downstream, on dancers, in rehearsal. A convincing preview moves the reckoning later — budget for it there.

docs.title: The assembled architecture
docs.text:
The whole synthesis fits in a paragraph. A small, typed, hand-authored gamut (content units plus connectors, state-changing verbs first-class). A sequencer owning an enumerated list of continuity dimensions and nothing else. A machine tier enforcing transition legality — window metric, symmetry quotiented out, expertise-scaled thresholds, one strongly connected component. A human gate with stated criteria, interest and feasibility kept distinct, throughput budgeted. A proposal medium chosen for the role you want the human to play. Seventy years of practice, one working diagram — and nothing in it that stops applying when the dancer is made of pixels, except the rehearsal room where policy 3 got solved.
